definition: Showing great energy and passionate devotion in pursuing a cause, belief or goal.
example: Her zealous study of bird calls filled three notebooks before the end of spring.
nuance: Zealous suggests intense, sometimes excessive commitment to a cause, while eager can mean simply wanting something to happen.
prompt: A hall monitor takes her school's new recycling rule very seriously.
options: The zealous monitor checked every trash can at lunch for stray plastic bottles.
The zealous monitor shrugged and let students toss bottles anywhere they pleased.
The zealous monitor resented that a classmate had won the school's recycling award.
The zealous monitor hesitated over every bin, unsure whether the rule mattered to her.
reasons: Tireless, intense effort on behalf of a rule shows fervent commitment to it.
Indifference to the rule is the opposite of fiery devotion.
Resenting another's success describes jealousy, a look-alike word with a different meaning.
Doubt about whether a cause matters shows no passion for it.

practice.prompt: A student joins the debate team in the middle of the school year.
options: The zealous newcomer stayed late each evening to research both sides of every topic.
The zealous newcomer skipped most practices and rarely opened the research packets.
The zealous newcomer made the team laugh with silly voices and goofy costumes.
The zealous newcomer agreed to join only after a friend begged her for a week.
reasons: Giving up free evenings to prepare shows energetic, wholehearted dedication.
Neglecting the work reveals a lack of interest, not intense enthusiasm.
Clownish silliness fits the look-alike zany, not devotion to a goal.
Joining reluctantly under pressure lacks the eager drive the word requires.
